lesson: Week 2, Lesson 4: Teaching AI your voice, so the writing sounds like you

beats.text: People can tell when a post was written by AI, even when they can't say why, and they scroll past it. For anything with your name on it, that costs you more than the time the AI saved.
You don't have to stop using AI. Write your voice down for it, so it has something to copy besides the average of the internet.
Find five to ten pieces you wrote yourself, before AI touched them. Messages to customers, old posts that did well, an email you were proud of, voice note transcripts.

Casual writing counts, and it's often the most like you. Amaka pulls eight: six WhatsApp replies to customers, one Instagram post from 2021 that got a lot of comments, and her voice note transcript from lesson two.

chapters.label: Have the model describe your voice

beats.text: Paste them into a fresh chat and ask it to describe your writing voice so another writer could copy it.
Ask it to cover sentence length, the words you use often, how you open and close, how formal you are, and anything you never do. Ask for your own lines as examples, and tell it not to flatter you.
Then read what comes back and correct it. Amaka's said she uses humour often. She doesn't. She's warm, which is different, so she changes that line.

chapters.label: Turn it into a voice skill

beats.text: Take the corrected description and make it a skill, using the template from week one.
Rules come from the description: short sentences, talk to one customer, mention real details like the area, the price, and what people said.
A Never section lists the words and habits you don't want, and it does the most work. What good looks like holds two or three of your real pieces, pasted as they are.
Call it something like my voice, and write the description in the words you'd actually type: use when I ask you to write, rewrite or edit anything that'll go out under my name.
These are the patterns that make writing read as machine-made. Put the ones you notice into your Never list.
Pet words, like delve, foster, leverage, seamless and tapestry. Fake contrast, like it's not just a cake, it's a memory, when you could say the true thing once.
Lists of three, every time. Openers that announce, like let's dive in. Tidy one-line endings on every paragraph.
Em dashes everywhere. And hedging and praise, like great question, or it's important to note that.
One last step in a fresh chat: mark every line in this that sounds like AI wrote it, and say why. Don't rewrite it. Then fix those lines yourself.
Your assignment this week: write one paragraph with the skill, then the same paragraph without it, and put them side by side.
If you can't tell them apart, your skill is too vague. Add more Never lines and one more real example, then try again.
